documents.abstract: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.

Time series forecasting supports decision-making in web applications such as online retail and network management, where planned actions can reshape future dynamics. World models provide a natural paradigm for predicting such action-dependent changes beyond extrapolating historical patterns. However, existing time series world models (TSWMs) typically rely on fixed, domain-specific covariate schemas that limit flexible intervention specification, while multimodal forecasters treat text primarily as passive predictive context. To investigate these gaps, we introduce TSWM-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark for multimodal TSWMs spanning seven real-world datasets, with textual interventions grounded in recorded action--outcome data. Our evaluation reveals that conventional multimodal forecasters underperform history-only time series foundation models (TSFMs) despite dataset-specific training, whereas simple text-prefix adaptations improve forecasting across all evaluated TSFM backbones. These findings suggest that pretrained TSFMs encode implicit world knowledge of temporal dynamics, offering a strong foundation for action-conditioned modeling beyond conventional multimodal fusion. Building on this insight, we propose TimeWorld, a plug-in framework that adapts pretrained TSFMs through explicit action-response modeling. Specifically, the Prototype-Guided Latent Modulation (PLM) module grounds textual actions in temporal dynamics by composing representative response prototypes to modulate future representations based on the action and historical patterns. The Action Contrastive Learning (ACL) component strengthens action-specific response modeling by contrasting these updates under alternative interventions sharing the same history, distinguishing action types while preserving relative intensity relationships.

We investigate whether limbic-like signatures of rapid, salience-driven behavior can be identified in high-resolution Counter-Strike 2 telemetry. This exploratory study introduces Ego-Knowledge, a leak-reduced reconstruction of each player's plausible perceptual state, supported by a millisecond-precision visibility engine and a reaction-centered extraction pipeline. Using a neuroscience-motivated 60--120 ms window, we derive coarse fight-or-flight labels from visibility- and damage-triggered events, with back-damage cases enabling constrained reaction-time analysis and manual label checks. We train two telemetry-native models using only information available by the trigger: EMBER (gradient boosting) and ORBIT (a custom transformer). On the full validation set, EMBER achieves 73.5% accuracy and ORBIT 71.2%, versus a 51.5% majority-class baseline, and both generalize to held-out players. The strongest LLM baseline achieves 62.7% on 1,000 validation cases; on these same cases, EMBER (73.6%) and ORBIT (70.9%) perform better (McNemar p=1.3e-9 and 1.5e-6, respectively), with orders-of-magnitude lower inference time and cost, though the comparison is not compute-matched. Including a short post-trigger window changes forecasting into early response recognition, raising accuracy monotonically to 85.15%. We propose this curve as a candidate probe of the transition from rapid to deliberative control, but roughly uniform per-tick gains do not establish that interpretation. The neuroscience framing is hypothesis-generating, not mechanistic: physiological ground truth, suitable control distributions, and reverse-inference limitations remain open. We outline extensions to auditory reconstruction, larger datasets, and telemetry-native foundation models.

Purpose of Review Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the tasks performed by physicians, raising questions about how graduate medical education should prepare trainees for future practice and whether residency workforce planning should change as AI adoption expands. This brief review examines the implications of AI for residency education and physician workforce planning, using radiology as an early model of technology-driven task transformation while considering broader effects across diagnostic, procedural, and relationship-based specialties. Recent Findings AI is already being used for clinical documentation, image interpretation, predictive analytics, administrative workflows, and large-scale data analysis. AI-assisted scribing has particular relevance to chronic pain and other documentation-intensive specialties, where it may reduce clerical burden and preserve clinician attention for patient care. However, current evidence more strongly supports task redistribution and physician augmentation than complete replacement. Specialties built around standardized digital information may experience earlier automation, whereas procedural skill, complex communication, longitudinal judgment, and responsibility for final clinical decisions remain difficult to substitute. At present, broad reductions in residency positions based only on anticipated AI capabilities seem premature. Summary Residency programs should adapt curricula now by incorporating AI literacy, verification skills, data interpretation, and safeguards against deskilling. Changes in residency position numbers should occur more cautiously and should be based on durable, specialty-specific workforce evidence, including hiring patterns, patient access, workload, productivity, and regional need. The goal should be to train physicians who can safely supervise and integrate AI while preserving the human expertise that remains central to high-quality care.

documents.abstract: Travel Mind AI is an intelligent travel planning system that combines Artificial Intelligence and map-based services to provide a personalized and convenient travel experience. The system assists users who are unsure about their destination by collecting details such as the number of travelers, budget, duration, and preferences, and then uses AI-powered APIs to recommend suitable destinations and travel plans. For users who have already decided on a destination, the system allows them to enter the source and destination locations and generates multiple possible routes using map services, arranging them based on distance with the shortest route displayed first. After selecting a route, the system displays it on an interactive map and identifies important facilities along or near the journey, such as petrol pumps, hotels, restaurants, hospitals, cafés, parking areas, and other points of interest. By integrating AI recommendations, route optimization, interactive maps, and location-based services, Travel Mind AI provides a complete travel planning and journey assistance solution that reduces the time and effort required to plan and manage a trip.

Abstract The International Global Atmospheric Chemistry (IGAC) Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report Phase II (TOAR-II) provides an updated, comprehensive assessment of the global distribution, burden and trends of tropospheric ozone, building on the foundation established by TOAR-I, 2014–2019. Accurate knowledge of tropospheric ozone concentrations remains essential for understanding atmospheric chemistry with far reaching implications for climate radiative forcing, vegetation damage and human health. Here, we present the process and summarize the main conclusions of TOAR-II, 2020–2026. Following TOAR-I, TOAR-II provides updates to trends in ozone concentrations and other metrics and addresses trends in ozone precursor emissions. This was accomplished as a community-driven process by forming Focus Working Groups to continue and expand on TOAR-I topics. Focus Working Group findings were published in a TOAR-II Community Special Issue with 58 review and original research papers. From this Community Special Issue, as well as other relevant literature, seven assessment papers were synthesized and submitted to this issue, along with this overview paper. These papers update the primary themes of TOAR-I: health, vegetation and climate; address unresolved uncertainties and inconsistencies in TOAR-I satellite ozone observations; provide an overdue update on stratosphere–troposphere exchange (STE) and present critical regional assessments for ozone over oceanic and polar regions, and South America. The TOAR-II assessment would not be possible without an extensive data collection and data harmonization effort. TOAR-II data are curated under findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable principles, and the TOAR data repository has been certified by the Core Trust Seal. In addition, TOAR-II developed common statistical analysis guidelines for the assessment papers. Although TOAR-II provides an extensive assessment of the current state of tropospheric ozone, many gaps and scientific challenges remain for future assessments. In particular, there is under-sampling of ozone across Southeast Asia and the Southern Hemisphere, especially Africa and Australia/Oceania. Low-cost sensor data and geostationary satellite data for tropospheric ozone, which still require evaluation, should be included. Ozone produced from wildfires and exacerbated by extreme weather events, and attribution of changes in ozone to pollution regulations on precursor emissions require greater attention in future analyses. These topics will be prioritized in the IGAC TOAR-III effort along with incorporating advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and strengthening collaboration with policy-relevant initiatives. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report II’.

All payloads synthetic or owner-generated; no customer-identifiable data appears in this record (POL-DISC-001). "Trust Is the Pollutant: Witness Receipts, Content-Addressed Storage, and the Environmental Case Against Redundant Copies." Global data centres consumed ~415 TWh in 2024 (~1.5% of world electricity, IEA Energy and AI 2025), projected past 1,000 TWh by 2030 in the Base Case. Not all of that energy buys information; some of it buys reassurance: the same artifact is routinely held hot by many parties because no party can cheaply prove any other party's copy is unaltered. This paper separates storage redundancy into availability-driven duplication (legitimate, retained) and trust-driven duplication (mechanically removable), and reports the measured production cost floor of removing the trust component with chain-witnessed content addressing: a 3,377-file corpus folded to an 80-byte Merkle root (MCR-4, root 38089f07...e8daaa) tri-chain anchored on Bitcoin OP_RETURN, Stellar manage-data, and XRP memo; a three-way fractional ownership transfer (FRACTAL-2, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23655614) witnessed byte-exact on three mainnets for $0.2509 measured ($0.1254 at the 1 sat/vB trough); and ~1.9 cents per receipt amortized via weekly BTC batching (SOV-B1, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23628676). Verification is keyless — any browser, any public explorer, no account, no platform, no custodian. Honest scoping: receipts shrink copies, not bytes; the canonical copy must still exist and be retrievable; retrieval becomes a commodity market ("who serves this hash cheapest") and every provider can win. UK/EU resonance: NESO-scoped UK data-centre demand growing from 3.6 TWh/yr (2020) toward 13–35 TWh/yr by 2050, and Great Britain's demand-connection queue rising from 41 GW (Nov 2024) to ~125 GW (June 2025), make connection-efficient dedup a grid resource; witness-verified cold-tiering is a measurable, auditable net-zero reduction whose proof is publicly verifiable rather than self-attested. Claimed (scoped): the measured cents-per-anchor tri-chain witness cost floor that makes custodian-free cross-party verification cheaper than the first guarded replica it displaces; the chain-as-witness architecture (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23649741) applied to shared-storage trust; the environmental framing of trust-driven duplication as purchased, avoidable energy; and receipts-first disclosure practice. The Section 5 savings illustration is labeled illustrative and scales with the true size of the trust-driven fraction, which this paper does not measure; the cost floor is measured. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in daily life, ascertaining whether an agent is human is critical. Here we systematically benchmark AI’s ability to imitate humans in three language tasks (image captioning, word association and conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection and attention prediction), collecting data from n = 636 humans and 37 AI agents. We also conducted 72,191 Turing-like tests with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges. Current AIs are approaching the ability to convincingly impersonate humans and deceive human judges in both language and vision. Even simple AI judges outperformed humans in distinguishing AI from human responses. Imitation ability showed minimal correlation with conventional AI performance metrics, suggesting that passing as human is an important independent evaluation criterion. The large-scale Turing-like datasets and metrics introduced here offer valuable benchmarks for assessing human-likeness in AI and highlight the importance of rigorous, quantitative imitation tests for AI development. Zhang et al. systematically compare humans and AI across three language and three vision tasks.

documents.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained entirely offline , without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated distribution over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from $$71.3\%$$ (FCFS) and $$84.1\%$$ (learning-to-rank) to $$90.4\%$$ , cuts P99 TTFT by up to $$3.3\times $$ , and reduces recompute/eviction events below $$1\%$$ , approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to examine how state public health agency governance and structure relate to recruitment systems such as hiring laws, recruitment barriers, and workforce practices. DESIGN: This cross-sectional study uses secondary data from the 2022 Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) Profile Survey and the 2023 Public Health Hiring Laws Dataset. Descriptive statistics and bivariate analyses were conducted to assess relationships between governance, structure, and recruitment systems. SETTING: State public health agencies in the United States. PARTICIPANTS: 50 US state health departments. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Associations between governance type (centralized, decentralized, mixed) and agency structure (free-standing vs. umbrella) with statutory hiring requirements, reported recruitment barriers, adoption of workplace practices, and distribution of responsibility for human resource (HR) functions. RESULTS: Governance and agency structure were not significantly associated with statutory hiring requirements, including use of hiring lists, civil service examinations, or merit-based criteria. Most reported recruitment barriers did not vary by governance or structure. One exception was difficulty advertising or engaging qualified applicants, which was reported more frequently among decentralized states compared with mixed governance states. Agency structure was associated with certain workforce practices: free-standing agencies were more likely than umbrella agencies to report employee recognition programs and physical wellness programs. Responsibility for HR functions was often shared between public health agencies and centralized administrative entities, with notable ambiguity in benefits administration, occupational health and safety, and labor relations. Agencies in which public health retained sole responsibility for selected HR functions were also more likely to report implementation of workforce development and employee engagement practices. CONCLUSIONS: Governance and agency structure were largely not associated with recruitment-related factors. However, variation in HR authority and workplace practices suggests organizational arrangements may shape workforce management. Strengthening the public health workforce may require aligning HR authority with workforce priorities alongside improvements to administrative infrastructure and hiring systems.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across tasks, but they still struggle with complex reasoning that requires integrating scattered knowledge. Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) addresses this challenge by organizing fragment knowledge as graphs, while recent Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) further improve GraphRAG with graph-native retrieval and reasoning capabilities. However, existing GraphRAG methods usually adopt decoupled retrieve-then-generate pipelines, which create objective misalignment between retrieval and reasoning, and training GFM retrievers typically depends on expensive human annotations. To address these limitations, we propose \ourmethod, a unified end-to-end GraphRAG framework that tightly couples a GFM retriever with an LLM generator. Given a query, the GFM retriever first reasons over the graph to score and retrieve relevant document nodes. These node embeddings are then passed through a fully differentiable graph bridge, which projects them into soft-weighted graph prefixes according to retrieval scores and combines them with raw document texts to form graph-augmented prompts. In this way, structural information is injected directly into LLM generation, while the final answer loss can be back-propagated through the bridge to jointly optimize retrieval and reasoning. To stabilize training and reduce reliance on costly annotations, we further introduce a semantic-guided distillation module that provides auxiliary supervision using pseudo-labels derived from query-document semantic similarities. Extensive experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets and three out-of-domain GraphRAG benchmarks show that \ourmethod consistently outperforms strong baseline methods and generalizes well, which demonstrates the effectiveness of end-to-end GraphRAG with tightly integrated GFM retrieval and LLM reasoning.

Game development stresses coding agents in ways general software engineering does not: correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact, not on source code alone. Existing benchmarks mainly target platforms such as Godot and heavily rely on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. We present UnityBench-Mini3D, a benchmark of 77 project-level Unity tasks organized around seven expert-defined skill categories rather than tutorials or genres, with three difficulty tiers. Each task pairs a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements and is evaluated using 1,178 held-out, human-authored milestone tests covering scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior. This in-engine evaluation provides deterministic partial credit, localizes failures, and distinguishes partial implementations from complete solutions without relying on subjective judges. Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate reaches 80.9% on easy tasks but falls to 35.2% on hard tasks, with just 57.7% overall. UnityBench-Mini3D provides a reproducible, diagnostic testbed distinguishing systems across difficulty levels.

Abstract While problems of AI systems are often attributed to technical shortcomings, some systems fail because they are built on ontologically and epistemologically “unstable ground.” Ground truth, or the datasets against which machine-learning systems are trained, validated, and tested, renders a particular representation of the world learnable by translating complex qualitative phenomena into mathematical formalisms. In doing so, it can stabilize tenuous truth claims while concealing fundamental flaws in how those phenomena are modeled, leaving systems unable to address the problems they are designed to solve. We examine this problem through a case study of Germany’s Dialect Identification Assistance System (DIAS), an automated language assessment system used in determining asylum applicants’ countries of origin. Drawing on Ground Truth Tracing (Kang 2023), we identify three reductions through which DIAS links speech to country of origin: treating language as code, mapping dialect onto bounded territory, and inferring nationality from this mapping. From linguistic and legal perspectives, these assumptions lack sufficient empirical grounding. DIAS may therefore produce internally coherent outputs while lacking the capacity to fulfil its intended task. We further argue that the EU AI Act is ill-equipped to detect such ontological flaws, as its risk-based framework evaluates systems against internally constructed ground truth rather than interrogating its aptitude to solve real-world problems. In asylum procedures, where such outputs may affect decisions on protection and return, these failures carry profound consequences.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Rapid urbanization and escalating waste generation are exerting significant pressure on existing urban infrastructure, necessitating scalable, intelligent, and multifunctional solutions. While current Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled smart bins primarily support waste monitoring and collection, their potential as integrated urban infrastructure remains largely untapped. This paper envisions the concept of Urban Intelligence Nodes (UINs), a new generation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled smart waste systems that extend beyond conventional waste management to serve as multi-functional nodes within a 6G-ready IoT ecosystem. The visioned UINs integrate AI, edge computing, and advanced wireless communication technologies to enable real-time waste classification, including hazardous object detection (e.g., explosive materials), thereby enhancing public safety and enabling timely alerts to emergency responders. In addition to safety applications, UINs are envisioned to function as distributed 6G micro base stations, environmental monitoring units for applications such as bushfire detection, and urban service platforms supporting infrastructure monitoring and aesthetic integration into city landscapes. By embedding intelligence and connectivity at the edge, UINs contribute to the realization of 6G networks as AI-native, ultra-reliable, and massively distributed systems. This position paper presents the architectural vision, enabling technologies, and key application domains of UIN-IoT, and discusses associated challenges, including security, privacy, scalability, and deployment considerations. It further highlights the transformative potential of UINs in redefining public waste infrastructure as a cornerstone of sustainable, secure, and connected smart cities.

documents.abstract: Synthetic supervision can bootstrap semantic parsers in new search domains, but prompt-induced diversity is useful only when generations are faithful to the structured intent. We explore this for cold-start e-commerce search: 118,098 synthetic pairs produced by 6 LLMs with 9 persona-conditioned prompt families on a 47-field UK automotive schema, against 1,214 human-annotated and 15,304 production queries. We show that the IPIP personality bundle improves parser F1 in all four matched contrasts (Holm-corrected $p<.001$), and all three bundles have a positive main effect over the complete $2^3$ grid. Syntax conditioning is the axis that moves generations towards real traffic. It also induces lexical diversity. Alignment sKL, the divergence between von Mises-Fisher distributions fitted to synthetic and human-annotated queries, is an unlabelled proxy for parser F1 ($ρ=-0.917$ against human queries written for simulated shopper scenarios, lower is closer). An LLM committee, checked against a blinded author pass, triages the 927 queries missed by every parser and labels 37% as hallucinated. Dropped constraints dominate. The four syntax-bearing families have the largest hallucinated shares, 38 to 42%, while IPIP alone has the lowest at 28%.

Perceived safety in public spaces is shaped by emotional, cognitive, social, and environmental factors, presenting a complex HCI design challenge. This study examines how women’s perceived safety varies across environmental contexts and how these experiences can inform context-aware smart wearable garments. A pilot study (n = 20) refined a 31-item questionnaire, followed by a main study of 199 valid respondents. A two-way ANOVA identified significant main effects of Gender and Living Environment on safety concern, with women reporting greater concern than men across Urban, Intra-urban, and Rural settings. PCA identified one dominant environmental-safety component containing three descriptive design factors: fear of physical harm, environmental discomfort, and socially situated risk. A second PCA identified Proactive Personal Safety and Environmental Awareness as priority smart-garment domains. These findings informed three design models and a proof-of-concept prototype linking user perception, environmental sensing, and adaptive feedback.

The swift progression of digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the educational landscape, creating both challenges and opportunities for asynchronous IT-related courses in public administration (PA) programs. For future public servants, such courses are not only vehicles for content delivery, but also spaces in which foundational competencies such as digital literacy, problem-solving, autonomous learning, and the effective use of technology in administrative contexts can be strengthened. This article outlines a framework for improving professor–student interaction and asynchronous course delivery, drawing on institutional research and relevant e-learning literature. It reports the outcomes of a university research project aimed at personalizing learning experiences through visual technologies, gamification, and AI-supported assistance, with particular attention to one introductory computer science course. The article presents an exploratory comparison of three naturally occurring cohorts of students in three consecutive academic years, examining how the staged integration of gamification and a GPT-4–based assistant coincided with changes in academic performance. The results show performance improvements across cohorts exposed to increasingly innovative delivery approaches. In a quasi-experimental comparison, exam performance improved following the staged introduction of gamification and AI-supported assistance, while the findings also suggest the broader pedagogical relevance of such tools for preparing PA students for digitally mediated professional environments.

This chapter explores how the United States Air Force (USAF) leader development course (LDC) used artificial intelligence (AI)/sentiment analysis (SA) for leader development and assessing leader development competencies that support learning objectives and course outcomes. A narrative format is first used to describe the engaged practice with key stakeholders and the staged approach process that underlaid the development of how innovation is driving change for leaders, assessing performance specific to selected competencies in mixed reality scenarios, and offering ways of strengthening leader development. A five-phased qualitative structure is used along with content analysis, design thinking, and a grounded theory approach. After coding data using thematic analysis from phases 1 to 4, a grounded theory approach is used to better understand the findings and discoveries with literature related to innovation development, AI technology associated with immersive learning environments, design thinking and change, performance and competency assessment, and leader development. A new theory (AI-augmented leader development theory) and a new model, emotionally tuned competency assessment model (ECAM), emerged as well as emphasis on the power of using dialogic development in virtual contexts to train, assess, and develop leaders. Theoretical and practical implications, as well as recommendations are provided for improving how AI tools can be used for leader development.

Abstract Purpose Understanding how much of routine policing involves vulnerable people could inform resourcing, training, and multi-agency response, yet administrative data provide limited insight. We explore whether an LLM-based classification pipeline, developed on open-source US police data, can be adapted to estimate the prevalence of four vulnerability indicators: mental ill health, substance misuse, alcohol dependence, and homelessness, in UK police incident narratives, and when outputs can be treated as defensible measurements. Methods We analyse nearly 3,000 de-identified incident logs from a UK police force, using a multi-stage pipeline combining repeated model inference, label aggregation, structured human review, and statistical correction. The pipeline runs on a locally hosted open-weight LLM, reflecting secure compute environments police are likely to use. Our approach assesses output stability, quantifies biases, and generates corrected estimates with uncertainty. Results LLMs can produce meaningful, if imperfect, prevalence estimates at scale. Mental ill health indicators are present in approximately one in five incidents, with lower prevalence for other indicators. However, naïve LLM deployment is unreliable: single-pass classifications are unstable, and aggregated outputs systematically over-assign indicators relative to human judgement. Correcting these biases required substantial human input and statistical adjustment, leaving considerable uncertainty. Conclusions While LLMs can extract information from unstructured police data, their outputs cannot be treated as valid measurements without careful methodological support. At the population level, defensible estimates are achievable but resource-intensive; at the individual level, errors remain frequent and unpredictable, limiting suitability for operational decisions. This study highlights the potential and constraints of LLM-based measurement, underscoring the need for rigorous evaluation in applied settings.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models increasingly act through code, modifying repositories, executing programs, and interacting with services in agent form. Their actions introduce risks that cannot be assessed from generated responses alone. Safety evaluation must verify actual consequences, distinguish harm avoidance from task incapability, and cover realistic workflows. We introduce V$^3$AST-Bench, a benchmark for Verifiable results, Valid interpretation, and Versatile risk coverage of Agent Safety. It comprises 212 risk tasks spanning 18 categories. Dedicated runtime environments verify harm and task outcomes through executable checks over states, records, and artifact behavior, while paired capability twin tasks verify workflow competence. Our experiments span 51 combinations of 11 models and five harnesses, spanning 86,496 trials and over 9 billion tokens of model interaction. Results show that V$^3$AST-Bench remains challenging even for frontier coding agents, as Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code still causes verified harm on 20.9% of tasks. Across model-harness combinations, agents with comparable competence exhibit markedly different safety outcomes, showing that task capability alone does not guarantee safe execution. More importantly, even explicit recognition of risks does not reliably prevent harmful actions, revealing a critical gap between risk awareness and safe execution. These findings highlight the need to move beyond risk recognition toward enforcing safety throughout execution.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AIM: To explore experiences of workplace violence among nurses and drivers working in prehospital emergency medical services in northeastern Italy. DESIGN: A qualitative interpretative study. METHODS: A qualitative interpretative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with a group of Italian healthcare professionals involved in out-of-hospital emergency care. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling and included nurses and ambulance drivers who had experienced at least one episode of workplace violence. Data were collected between May and August 2025 and analysed using inductive content analysis. RESULTS: Fifteen participants were interviewed. Three main themes were developed: 'Violence is taken home', 'Microaggressions: the invisible violence', and 'Strategies: Si vis pacem, para violentiam'. Workplace violence had lasting emotional and professional consequences including fear, helplessness, and reduced well-being. Microaggressions, often normalized and influenced by gender and cultural factors, were under-recognized forms of violence. Participants described using communication and de-escalation techniques, situational awareness, and peer support, while perceiving organizational support as insufficient. CONCLUSION: Workplace violence in prehospital emergency care has significant emotional and professional consequences and may be underreported. Microaggressions represent an important, often overlooked dimension requiring recognition and intervention. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Targeted training in communication and violence management, improved reporting systems, and structured psychological support are essential to mitigate the impact of workplace violence. Promoting a supportive organizational culture and addressing microaggressions may enhance staff well-being, patient safety, and quality of care. IMPACT: Addressing both overt violence and normalized microaggressions, alongside strengthening organizational support, is essential to safeguarding healthcare professionals in prehospital emergency settings. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No Patient or Public Contribution. REPORTING METHOD: The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Studies (COREQ) checklist was used.

Vision-language foundation models (VLFMs) for medical image understanding have advanced rapidly, yet evidence supporting clinical deployment remains fragmented. This narrative review synthesizes architectures, training paradigms, benchmarks, public datasets, and translation barriers. Drawing on more than 50 original studies published between 2020 and 2025, we provide a structured descriptive comparison rather than a statistical meta-analysis. In a focused audit of 13 representative studies, BLEU/ROUGE was reported by 31% (4/13), RadGraph F1 by 0% (0/13), CheXpert- or CheXbert-derived label evaluation by 46% (6/13), BERTScore by 8% (1/13), human expert evaluation by 31% (4/13), and inference latency or throughput by 0% (0/13). Because datasets, splits, candidate pools, and metrics differ, cross-task results are presented as exploratory benchmark indicators and not as a clinical-readiness scale. The synthesis identifies persistent concerns involving hallucination, limited interpretability, distribution shift, and narrow demographic and geographic coverage. We propose a minimum clinical validation and reporting standard aligned with the distinct purposes of FDA/Health Canada/MHRA and IMDRF Good Machine Learning Practice, the EU AI Act, TRIPOD+AI, and CLAIM, and identify eleven priority research directions. Medical VLFMs are promising, but progress should be judged by source-traceable, clinically grounded, and externally validated evidence.

documents.abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.

The growing use of intelligence in legal research has opened new chances for speed yet it has also sparked worries about how accurate and trustworthy legal authorities are. These worries were highlighted in the case of Pooja Ramesh Singh versus Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. In that case the Supreme Court of India looked at how the National Company Law Tribunal had used fabricated and artificial intelligence‑generated material. The core dispute was about enforcing a guarantee but the Supreme Court's ruling brought up a wider issue: how can courts stay honest if they rely on fake authorities as legal precedent? This paper looks at the facts of the case the Supreme Court's reasoning and what it means for lawyers, judges and the whole legal field. It points out the line between using artificial intelligence as a research helper and treating artificial intelligence output as an official source of law. The paper also talks about the duty of lawyers to check citations. The need for courts and tribunals to verify the authenticity of the authorities they see. Even though artificial intelligence can make research faster this paper says that convenience cannot replace careful work or judicial responsibility. The Supreme Court's decision reaffirms that legal choices must be based on trustworthy sources of law. It also asks questions about fair disciplinary actions and the safeguards that are needed as artificial intelligence grows in law practice. In the end this paper says that while technology can help thinking the responsibility, for the correctness and honesty of legal papers must stay with human professionals.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely discussed in higher education in relation to learning, assessment design, and academic integrity. Much of this discussion, however, treats students’ AI use as a set of discrete academic practices, rather than as part of broader decision-making that spans learning and everyday life. This piece argues that students’ academic and non-academic uses of AI increasingly shape one another, influencing how they approach uncertainty, manage emotional pressure, and make judgements when learning feels high stakes. Drawing on academic advising and personal tutoring conversations, it shows that students are not using AI solely to generate outputs, but to talk ideas through, test interpretations, and steady their thinking when confidence and academic identity are in play. These practices closely resemble the relational and cognitive work advisers already support and make visible how AI is now being used to sustain the emotional work of learning that underpins sound judgement. A practice-based framework is presented describing four overlapping modes of student AI use - instrumental, dialogic, metacognitive, and affective-regulatory - each aligned with established advising functions. Rather than positioning AI as a threat to academic integrity or professional judgement, the paper argues for advising as guidance: supporting students to recognise how AI shapes their thinking, to develop appropriate boundaries, and to make learning decisions with confidence and responsibility.

documents.abstract: Generative AI can produce code, tests, documentation, and technical explanations that resemble artefacts traditionally used as evidence of student competence, weakening the inference from artefact quality to the engineering capability behind it. We report the redesign and first deployment of a 13-week, AI-permissive, software-intensive engineering course in which students may delegate substantial work to AI while retaining responsibility for planning, verification, review, integration, and explanation. The redesign couples an engineering accountability workflow, which structures human-AI work and preserves human decision authority, with an assessment evidence architecture comprising six complementary channels: product, process/origin, verification, explanation, reflection, and individual assurance. A collect--cross-check--escalate (CCE) reasoning logic connects these channels rather than treating any single artefact or trace as sufficient evidence of competence. By the end of Week 11, the deployment involved 87 students organised into 17 teams, with 957 individual weekly Git repositories and 34 group-project Git repositories supporting repeated assessment and engineering activity. The first deployment yielded four practical lessons: AI assistance changes where rubric criteria carry evidential weight; multiple evidence channels require deliberate cross-checking and meaningful complementarity; the evidential strength realised in practice may differ from that intended in the assessment design; and automation scales evidence collection more readily than interpretation. The contribution is a conceptually grounded, deployed design for making engineering responsibility and competence more visible when AI can perform substantial artefact production.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for training multimodal agents to reason and use tools. However, it remains unclear when fine-grained credit assignment improves learning and when it fails to improve task performance. Video editing provides a useful testbed for this question, combining multimodal perception, long-horizon planning, and tool use with delayed outcome feedback. We construct four movie-trailer editing task types---Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, Rough Cut, and Fine Cut---that reflect real-world editing workflows and span different levels of task complexity and interaction horizon. Decaying process rewards provides the largest benefit on Fine Cut, with a 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on tasks averaging more than 60 turns under outcome-only GRPO. On the three shorter-horizon task types averaging 30--40 turns under the same baseline, outcome-only GRPO remains competitive, with decaying process rewards yielding at most a 10.4% relative gain. Process rewards from an LLM judge initially improve tool use and encourage visual inspection. As training progresses, however, GRPO+PRM with a fixed process-reward weight increasingly exhibits excessive reasoning and redundant tool calls: process rewards continue to rise while task completion rates and outcome scores decline. Decaying the process-reward weight to zero mitigates this reward-hacking behavior while preserving the early gains. Despite dense token-level supervision, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) yields little improvement or substantial degradation and is highly sensitive to the choice of privileged information. Our analysis reveals differences in teacher--student disagreement and gradient magnitudes, and suggests possible dilution of informative signals over long trajectories.

Machine translation (MT) and artificial intelligence (AI) are used in an ad hoc manner to negotiate intercultural communication in health care settings. As AI is currently subject to public debate, it is important to consider perceptions of and discourses around it. Through a literature review of translation and interpreting studies and health sciences, this article first explores some challenges that MT and AI pose, along with the persistence of reductive thinking around language and the role of the interpreter. It then develops a qualitative content analysis of 41 semi-structured interviews with health care and intercultural communication actors in Catalonia. Informants view MT and AI as useful for simple, low-stakes communication while preferring humans. Despite this, there is an ‘acquiescent anxiety’ around the unstoppable progress of science. In addition, there is a tendency to distinguish between ‘mere’ translation and other ‘added value’ activities, like intercultural mediation. We argue that, when interpreters are not merely thought of as machines, but really are machines, the relentless reduction of interpreting to ‘mechanical parroting’ paves the way for its automatisation. On the flipside, informants reclaim an expanded interpreter role that involves knowledge of language, culture, medicine, the sociology of health and illness, social science methodologies and ethical intercultural communication.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming embedded in higher education, yet their benefits may be unevenly distributed. This study conceptualizes prompt engineering competence (PEC) as an equity-relevant interaction competence and examines whether differences in PEC are associated with perceived academic gains and perceived educational inequity. We adopt a two-stage quantitative design combining a cross-sectional survey with a within-subject prompt-quality experiment. Stage 1 reports a survey of Chinese undergraduates who have used LLMs ( N = 380), measuring PEC, perceived academic performance gains, perceived educational inequity, family digital capital, gaming experience, and a planning/independent-work tendency. Regression and mediation analyses show that PEC was strongly associated with perceived academic gains, while its association with perceived inequity was statistically significant but small. Background resources and learning-related experiences and dispositions explained substantial variance in PEC, especially gaming experience and planning/independent-work tendency, and the association between family digital capital and perceived academic gains was largely indirect through PEC. Stage 2 conducts a within-subject prompt-quality experiment across four higher-education task types and four popular models, comparing basic prompts with a student-oriented five-component refined prompt framework (Role–Goal–Input–Process–Output). Analysis of 400 matched prompt comparisons, comprising 800 model outputs, indicates that the refined prompt scaffold consistently outperforms basic prompts. Overall, the findings identify PEC as a potential competence pathway through which students may differ in their ability to convert LLM access into learning-related benefits, while structured prompt scaffolds may provide a scalable approach to reducing prompt-quality barriers in LLM-supported higher education.

documents.abstract: Abstract Problem. On social media platforms and search engines, what becomes visible, and what goes viral, is decided by recommendation, ranking, and amplification algorithms. During elections, referendums, declared public emergencies, and other internal crises, a change in the algorithmic configuration that actually runs can alter the reach of civic information at national scale within hours. Once an item has been amplified to millions of people, the effect cannot be undone. Where present solutions fall short. Today’s accountability rests on deployment approvals, model version records, signed software, audit logs, and periodic compliance reviews. These records show what was approved or what was installed. They do not show which configuration actually produced a particular ranked feed or recommendation. They also cannot stop an unauthorized output before it reaches users. A configuration can be approved upstream while a fallback model, experiment router, cache, or edge service substitutes, reorders, or redirects the output on an unverified path. Retrospective audit can find such a change only after the amplification has already happened. Solution. This work describes an implementation-neutral architecture built on the Algorithmic Logic Fingerprint (ALF), which has three parts: ALF-I identifies an authorized algorithmic configuration. ALF-E records protected measurements of the components and configurations that actually executed. ALF-O binds that execution evidence to a specific pending output. A protected validation domain issues a cryptographically authenticated validation receipt. Authority to make the output effective is set up separately as a scoped, non-bearer finality enablement. An independent Finality Sink at the effectuation boundary (gateway, CDN or edge, network egress, or device rendering) reconstructs the actual pending operation. It then checks the receipt, the enablement, the current crisis-mode generation, revocation state, and route coverage, and consumes the authority atomically before permitting the output. When any check fails, the output is withheld rather than delivered. What is new. The architecture treats algorithmic virality as a sequence of individually verifiable amplification operations. It separates computation, validation, and authority: computation is not authority to make an output effective. It models internal crises as authenticated, generation-numbered operating modes that untrusted workloads cannot switch. Organic speech is protected structurally. A failed algorithmic amplification check does not block a user’s direct publication. Heterogeneous proprietary algorithms can be verified without requiring a common ranking model and without disclosing source code, model weights, or ranking parameters. The work sets out 22 enforcement points across model activation, distributed ranking stages, delivery routes, streaming feeds, and device displays. It also provides a structured counter-verification procedure for disputed decisions. Its technical relevance is discussed for the EU Digital Services Act (Articles 34, 35, 37, and 40), the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Articles 9 and 12 to 15), India’s Information Technology Act, 2000, with the Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021, as amended, and the WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (Articles 2.1, 2.2, and 2.4). These references describe possible technical relevance only and do not establish legal compliance. The architecture does not prescribe political viewpoints, judge the truthfulness of speech, or require algorithmic uniformity: algorithmic accountability does not require algorithmic uniformity. This work makes no allegation of electoral manipulation, unlawful interference, or regulatory violation by any platform, company, government, political organization, or individual. documents.abstract: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 defers the AI Act's obligations for high-risk employment systems to December 2027, a year after Member States must transpose the Platform Work Directive. The order in which EU rules on algorithmic management reach the workplace has been inverted, and the first national implementing measures are being adopted in the interval. Poland's Act of 3 July 2026 is one of them. This development note examines what it does with the obligation in Article 26(7) AIA, which requires employers to inform workers’ representatives before putting a high-risk system into service and refers the manner of doing so back to national law. Drawing on the two rounds of consultation on the Polish bill, it shows that the Ministry refused trade union representation on the new supervisory Commission on the ground that the Labour Inspectorate sat on it as a permanent member, and that the inspectorate was removed four months later, at its own request, invoking ILO Convention No 81. The refusal stood; the reason for it did not. The episode illustrates a problem that the Union instruments do not address: representation that is present on paper, relied upon to answer objections and then withdrawn.

Large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents can synthesise scientific arguments and construct computational models rapidly, but fluency is not scientific validity. Neither expert status, human oversight, multi-agent consensus, publication nor patent protection substitutes for independent empirical testing. Experiments themselves can conflict because of bias, measurement error or genuine biological heterogeneity. We propose an evidence-to-decision trust architecture for drug research and model-informed drug development (MIDD) that links verifiable primary observations, provenance and uncertainty to competing mechanistic hypotheses, adversarial AI review, discriminating experiments and accountable decisions. Credibility is evaluated for a specified context of use, not assigned globally to people or algorithms. The framework spans target validation, translational pharmacology, dosing, clinical development and regulatory assessment, illustrated by a proposed IQANOVA ATLAS AI–quantitative systems pharmacology (AI-QSP) workflow. We extend the framework to regulatory agencies using AI agents: scientific assessment and model credibility are distinct from the legally binding act of medicine authorisation. Inspired by Juvenal's question of who checks the guardians and the historical Rabkrin inspection debate, we propose auditable agent roles, explicit legal decision rights, independent scrutiny and routes for challenge. A synthetic SBML/SED-ML/COMBINE package with provenance ontologies illustrates reproducible reporting without claiming biological validation. A prospective benchmark is proposed to test scientific quality, regulatory decision loss, agent independence and appeal outcomes. The final question—whether, when and under whose authority an AI could make binding decisions—remains unresolved.
