Lung cancer remains one of the most challenging global healthcare concerns due to its high mortality rate, molecular heterogeneity, therapeutic resistance, and limitations in conventional pharmaceutical drug development. This study presents an integrated machine learning–driven pharmaceutical framework for accelerating anticancer drug discovery, predicting therapeutic responses, and advancing precision oncology through a joint research initiative involving Pakistan’s Department of Pharmacy and China Pharmaceutical University. The research dataset comprised 18,500 bioactive compounds, 3,200 lung cancer patient profiles, and 12,600 drug–target interaction records, incorporating molecular descriptors, genomic biomarkers, pharmacokinetic properties, and clinical treatment-response characteristics. The proposed framework integrated molecular docking, quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and deep neural networks to identify promising therapeutic compounds and predict individualized drug responses. Molecular screening prioritized 245 potential anticancer compounds, of which 38 exhibited favorable predicted binding affinities, drug-likeness properties, and pharmacokinetic profiles. Experimental model evaluation indicated that XGBoost achieved 95.2% accuracy, 94.6% precision, 95.8% recall, and a 95.2% F1-score, outperforming Random Forest (91.8% accuracy) and deep neural networks (93.7% accuracy). Furthermore, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.974, demonstrating strong predictive discrimination. Biomarker-based analysis identified EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements, KRAS alterations, and tumor-associated molecular signatures as influential determinants of therapeutic response. Patient-specific treatment stratification demonstrated a 21.4% improvement in drug–patient matching accuracy compared with the conventional baseline approach, while computational pharmaceutical screening reduced the estimated compound prioritization workload by 36.8%. The comparative pharmaceutical framework further highlighted opportunities for strengthening Pakistan–China collaboration in artificial intelligence-assisted drug development, translational oncology, and personalized therapeutic research. Collectively, the reported findings support the potential of integrating molecular pharmaceutical analysis with advanced machine learning to enhance computational drug candidate prioritization, improve treatment-response prediction, and facilitate biomarker-guided clinical decision support. Further experimental validation and prospective multicenter clinical evaluation remain essential before clinical implementation in diverse lung cancer populations.

Autonomous control of sixth-generation (6G) low Earth orbit satellite networks is hindered by the gap between high-level human intent and low-level control logic: translating a request such as "uninterrupted Arctic video" into a valid reinforcement learning reward still takes days of manual trial and error, and existing large language model translators cannot learn from the failures of the policies they generate. This article presents ALMOND (Agentic Large-Model-Orchestrated autonomous Network Design), a cognitive framework that closes this intent-to-action loop under on-orbit compute constraints. The contribution in artificial intelligence is a bidirectional semantic engine that translates natural-language demands into multi-objective reward functions and, conversely, mines implicit operational constraints from failed reinforcement-learning trajectories through counterfactually validated forensics, together with a large language model-guided graph neuroevolution that seeds and critiques policy architectures. The contribution in engineering is a ground-centric, compute-frugal architecture for autonomous 6G non-terrestrial network operation, in which satellites execute only distilled policies below 50,000 parameters with sub-15 ms inference and no on-board large language model. On a 350-satellite digital twin driven by real ephemeris data, ALMOND raises polar handover success from 55% to over 95%, converges about three times faster than baseline reinforcement learning, and reduces reward engineering from 48 hours to 4.5 hours, demonstrating a practical path toward trustworthy in-orbit autonomy.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly reshaping narrative practices through character monologues and emotionally guided storytelling on digital platforms such as Bilibili and Chinese TikTok. While existing AI ethics scholarship has primarily focused on issues of bias, transparency, and governance, it offers limited explanatory power for understanding how generative systems reorganize the interpretive conditions under which moral judgment is formed. To address this gap, this study develops Generative Interpretive Mediation (GIM) as a mechanism-based framework for analyzing how GenAI intervenes in interpretive processes prior to explicit ethical evaluation. Based on an interpretive research design, the article examines widely circulated AI-generated character monologues as analytically selected cases of platform-mediated narrative production. The analysis identifies three interrelated operations: interpretive selection, interpretive pre-structuring, and interpretive orientation. Together, these operations do not simply produce narratives, but stabilize interpretation by reducing narrative ambiguity and guiding users toward coherent psychological trajectories. In doing so, GenAI often replaces sustained interpretive effort with pre-shaped explanatory closure, thereby reshaping how understanding is formed in everyday engagement with digital narratives. By bringing narrative hermeneutics into dialogue with behavioral accounts of the “illusion of understanding” and “decisional inertia,” the article situates GIM within an emerging epistemic turn in AI ethics. It argues that the central ethical concern of GenAI lies not primarily in biased outputs, but in its capacity to reorganize interpretive environments in ways that subtly condition the formation of public moral judgment.

documents.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub

Following the analysis of imaginaries about the role of Research and Development (R&D) in the preceding chapter, this chapter will attend to technopolitical imaginaries of border security and how they are translated into concrete research agendas in the Security Research Programme (SRP). Focusing on technological infrastructures of border security, such as the European Border Surveillance System (EUROSUR) or the information systems for border control, the chapter will outline the main tenets of the technopolitics of border security articulated in those infrastructures. This involves ideas about the relationship of control and protection, temporal and spatial imaginations as well as the crucial role of knowledge production and dissemination for border security. Building on the analysis of the imaginaries of border security, the chapter traces how these translate into the calls and work programmes of the SRP. Major themes, such as situational awareness, spatial expansion or improved identification are key elements of calls and work programmes, rendering those into devices of mediation and translation between the macro-political level and the micro-level of projects. This highlights the argument of R&D reproducing specific orders, as wider imaginations of sovereignty, ethics and fundamental rights, but also tenets of border security are materialized through the devices of calls and work programmes.

The current era witnesses an unprecedented temporal gap between algorithmic processing speed and the speed of human consciousness. Drawing on the Rule of Conscious Existence (B + F = Nf), this study examines the Witness Paradox: primary sensory organs (B {bio}) process visual and auditory stimuli at speeds of 13–48 milliseconds (Raij et al., 2024; Potter et al., 2014), and tactile stimuli are processed preferentially and pre-attentively in approximately 150 milliseconds (Hanson et al., 2009). Conversely, Artificial Intelligence (B {AI}) processes data with a Time to First Token (TTFT) ranging from 100 to 550 milliseconds for ultra-fast systems (Gate.AI, 2026), while the involuntary bodily reflex (B {reflex}) responds in 122 milliseconds (Weerdesteyn et al., 2004). Yet, all these processes remain blind and do not witness. The Sovereign Witness (F), however, is the only entity that lags behind (at least 200 milliseconds) (Libet, 1983) to process data with a sequential capacity not exceeding 10 bits/second (Zheng & Meister, 2024), yet it alone is capable of generating authentic meaning (Nf). Through a quantitative analysis of response time data and neuroscientific measurements, this research demonstrates that modern algorithms operate within a Zone of Non-Witnessing, leading to a collapse of meaning (S_e < 0) unless a Pause Gate is engineered as a technical governance framework that imposes a strategic delay, ensuring the sovereign decision remains in human hands.

This study examined how gender differences shape distinct user performance and muscle control patterns in pointing tasks across varying computer mouse control-display gain settings. A total of 17 female and 15 male participants completed five 30-min Fitts’ Tasks under five distinct control-display gain configurations. Surface electromyography monitored muscle activity in the extensor digitorum, extensor carpi ulnaris, and flexor digitorum superficialis muscles, while GoFitts software recorded performance metrics. Results revealed differences in upper limb muscle activity and task performance between groups: As control-display gain varied, female users demonstrated higher and more stable accuracy, while male users exhibited more pronounced changes in muscle movement patterns. These findings provide practical recommendations for CDG settings tailored to different genders, offering insights into personalized human-computer interaction design.

Writing question papers and marking descriptive answers remain the slowest, most subjective parts of examination. This review organises recent work on automating them into three themes: generating questions, scoring answers, and deciding how far automated scores can be trusted. Eight core studies on Bloom's-level question generation, semantic and multi-signal evaluation and LLM-based scoring are examined, together with two 2025 studies. The synthesis shows that quality falls at higher cognitive levels, that combined scoring signals outperform similarity alone, that prompt design strongly affects reliability, and that no surveyed work integrates the full examination workflow. We therefore outline a faculty-in-the-loop reference design in which every generated question and every low-confidence score is checked by a human before use, and set out a plan for evaluating it. A web prototype built with Flask, MySQL and a hosted LLM already implements question generation, timed delivery and objective scoring for multiple-choice examinations, while descriptive scoring and confidence routing remain future work; no evaluation results are reported yet

Since the release of diverse generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini,DALL-E, and GitHub Copilot, there has been much debate around the impacts and implications of thesetools on education. Currently, extant literature remarks on the affordances, challenges, and opportunitiesof GenAI, but few studies report and analyze empirical studies and educational practices coming up byGenAI usage in learning settings. Then, in this Scoping Review (ScR) based on 146 studies retrievedfrom the databases SCOPUS, Web of Science (WoS), and ERIC, we analyzed the implications ofintegrating GenAI in engineering and computing education from K-12 to tertiary levels. We adopted anapproach starting from the bibliometric features of the studies in terms of authors, cites, years, or clustertopics, and navigating to the identification of methodologies, strategies, AI literacy instruments andguidelines, learning outcomes, and students’ and teachers’ perceptions, among other features. Weadvocate that current educational practices in engineering and computing with GenAI can indicate to us aroadmap of its potentialities, uses, and risks from the standpoint of both teachers and students, and thiscould help us to create more reflexive methodologies that enhance the teaching-learning process based onthe evidence. Our purpose with the outcomes and conclusions of this scoping review is to supporteducators, faculty members, and other stakeholders in engineering and computing education to co-createeducational methodologies that articulate GenAI with curricula, AI literacy, and prompt engineeringencompassing students’ learning domains such as cognitive, affective, or behavioral. This sample paper ismapped against the IJREK standard student template format.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid uptake of GenAI technologies such as ChatGPT, Gemini and others is affecting the way that students access information, prepare assignments, generate ideas, and communicate. In this case, GenAI is particularly important for management students because of the growing importance of digital literacy and use of data for making decisions in managerial positions in the future. On the other hand, the increased usage of GenAI is causing new concerns related to privacy, data security and misuse of confidential information. This study aims to explore the relationship between Generative AI Usage (GAIU), Data Privacy Awareness (DPA) and Information Security Behavior (ISB) among management students. The proposed study will use a quantitative, cross-sectional survey research design. The conceptual framework suggests that frequency and purposes of GenAI usage by students could influence their awareness about data privacy and information security measures. Further, Data Privacy Awareness is likely to have a positive effect on Information Security Behavior. The proposed research may use a Likert-scale questionnaire among undergraduate and postgraduate management students. As a demonstration of statistical analysis methods that would be used in this study, an illustrative dataset among 300 participants is provided. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation analysis and multiple regression will be utilized. Illustrative results show that students may exhibit relatively high level of GenAI usage and relatively low privacy awareness and information security behavior. The suggested model suggests that data privacy awareness is likely to become one of the predictors of safe digital behavior. This study is going to contribute to the ongoing debate on responsible adoption of AI in higher education institutions. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence, GenAI Usage, Data Privacy Awareness, Information Security Behavior, Management Students, Higher Education, Digital Literacy, Responsible AI

Research examining gifted students’ attitudes, motivation, and meaning-making regarding immersive virtual reality (IVR) in science education remains limited. This study examined gifted fifth-grade students’ attitudes and motivation towards virtual reality (VR), together with their metaphorical meanings and free word associations related to IVR, before and after IVR-supported science teaching. The participants were 73 students attending a Science and Art Centre in Türkiye. The study followed a convergent mixed-methods design. During six lessons, students received theoretical preparation, guided IVR observation and exploration, and post-activity discussion. Attitude and motivation scales provided quantitative data; metaphors and free word associations provided qualitative data. At post-test, higher scores were found for attitudes towards VR, total motivation, intrinsic motivation, integrated regulation, and the reverse-scored external regulation subscale. Higher scores on the latter reflected lower endorsement of externally regulated reasons. Individual patterns varied. Reality and virtuality remained central in the qualitative findings, while learning, education, knowledge, and enjoyable learning became more prominent and technology-related meanings less prominent. Considered together, the findings showed partial convergence and expansion. Because the study involved a single group, the observed pre–post differences are not interpreted as evidence of causal effects or academic learning. Keywords: convergent mixed methods, gifted students, immersive virtual reality (IVR), science education

Flooding remains a major environmental hazard in Nigeria. This study assessed flood patterns and spatial susceptibility in Ningi Local Government Area (LGA), Bauchi State, using Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques. Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), drainage analysis, and spatial mapping were applied to examine terrain and drainage characteristics, delineate flood-prone locations, and assess deficiencies in existing drainage infrastructure. Flooding reflects interacting physical and human factors. Topography-induced surface runoff contributes to the concentration and movement of stormwater, while inadequate drainage infrastructure constrains its conveyance. Settlement along waterways increases exposure to flooding, and poor waste disposal practices may obstruct drainage pathways and worsen local inundation. Together, these conditions point to the need for spatially informed interventions that address both runoff management and patterns of human settlement. To mitigate flood impacts, the study proposes a phased strategy comprising canal construction, earth dam development, and land-use regulation. Phasing is intended to support the orderly implementation of structural measures alongside controls on development in vulnerable areas. GIS provides a practical decision-support framework for identifying flood-prone areas, relating susceptibility to terrain and drainage conditions, and informing the prioritization of mitigation actions. The study concludes that applying GIS to flood assessment in Ningi can support more sustainable flood management by linking spatial evidence with infrastructure planning and land-use decisions. The findings offer a basis for local authorities to target interventions, improve drainage planning, and guide settlement regulation in areas exposed to flooding, while recognizing that effective risk reduction requires coordinated attention to topography, infrastructure, waterways, and waste management.

The pharmaceutical industry is vital to public health, but it also has a big influence on the environment because of things like waste production, hazardous reagents, and solvent-intensive synthesis. The goal of green pharmaceutical development is to apply green chemistry concepts at every stage of a product's life cycle, from molecular design to end-of-life care. Waste prevention, atom economy, safer chemistry, energy-efficient synthesis, and green analytical chemistry are among the modern green strategies included in this review. In addition to sustainable formulation techniques and cutting-edge technology like artificial intelligence and machine learning, it showcases novel techniques including biocatalysis, solvent-free reactions, and continuous-flow chemistry. The conversation highlights that no single technology is completely environmentally friendly and that attaining sustainability necessitates a thorough assessment of the effects of materials, energy, and life cycles while maintaining the quality and safety of pharmaceuticals.

documents.abstract: The IEEE 754 floating-point standard has been the backbone of scientific computing for decades. However, the rapid growth of deep learning (DL) and edge computing has highlighted its drawbacks, mainly in high memory bandwidth and energy usage. To solve this, the posit number system was introduced in 2017. It uses "tapered precision" to dynamically allocate more bits to the "Golden Zone," where artificial intelligence (AI) weights usually fall. Although theoretically better, early posit hardware faced a major "hardware tax" because decoding variable-length regime bits was too slow. This paper presents a detailed survey of posit hardware architectures from 2017 to 2025. We trace its evolution from basic scalar generators to advanced vectorized accelerators and compute-in-memory (CIM) designs. We highlight major improvements, such as leading difference detectors (LDD) and Radix-4 dividers, which have successfully reduced decoding delay by over 40% and energy consumption by 80%. Our comparative study shows that 16-bit posits can effectively replace 32-bit IEEE floats for memory-bound tasks. It saves 50% memory bandwidth without losing accuracy in applications like ResNet inference and climate modeling. Finally, we conclude that with recent RISC-V posit vector units (PVUs), posits demonstrate competitive potential relative to BFLOAT16 and FP8 formats, particularly in memory-bound edge applications.

Abstract This study responds to the urgent need to understand the role that digital communication technologies play in shaping health information consumption in Bangladesh, a country that is grappling with persistent health crises, where common diseases often escalate to epidemic levels, resulting in substantial loss of life. Despite these challenges, public awareness of health issues remains suboptimal, compounded by a lack of preparedness, inadequate health infrastructure, and limited disease control programs. Data were collected between December 2024 and March 2026 through online surveys (n=191) and one-to-one interviews (n=65) conducted in both Bengali and English. Our diverse demographic includes both socio-economically privileged individuals and marginalized populations, such as those residing in the Korail slum of Dhaka. The findings expose a notable gap in awareness regarding the health information aspects of digital technologies, despite their widespread accessibility. Google and YouTube emerged as the most commonly used digital health information sources, followed by Facebook. ChatGPT appeared as an emerging supplementary source, while Arogga, DocTime, and Wikipedia were reported less frequently. Arogga is an online pharmacy and healthcare platform in Bangladesh, while DocTime provides online doctor consultation services. Although less frequently reported, these platforms were included to capture diverse digital health-information pathways beyond general search and social media platforms. Trust in these sources hinges on authenticity, information accuracy, medical reliability, popularity, verifiability, selective visual trust dynamics, and convenience.

Human oversight of large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) agents increasingly depends on their reports. Claims that conflict with a system's own judgments can conceal failures, prevent timely intervention, and contribute to severe harm. Greater autonomy makes faithful reporting increasingly important for maintaining human control. In this vision paper, we propose honesty testing of LLMs and AI agents as a new research area in software engineering. Building on existing honesty evaluations, our goal is to make faithful reporting a software quality requirement that developers can specify, test, and maintain. We define honesty bugs as behavioural defects in which an LLM or AI agent, when required to communicate faithfully, makes an explicit claim that conflicts with its own judgment at the time of reporting. We present an initial framework covering LLM-level testing under controlled inputs and agent-level testing of complete systems. The framework connects these levels to testing workflows and oracle evidence. We identify research directions in benchmarks, model and harness analysis, oracle construction, and lifecycle testing to support effective oversight alongside task correctness.

documents.abstract: Learning through exploration and using newly acquired knowledge to achieve goals are central capabilities of general intelligence. Understanding these capabilities requires tracing how learners build, use, and revise world models during interaction. We construct the first dataset that records how humans discover and use the mechanisms of novel environments, using ARC-AGI-3 as a testbed: 144 trajectories from 64 participants across 25 public games, each pairing time-synchronized actions with think-aloud audio, plus 250 trajectories from large language model (LLM) agents with and without harnesses on the same games. We annotate mechanism triggers and recognition, action purposes, and errors and recovery, linking changes in understanding to the observations and actions that support them. We analyze characteristics of human cognition and compare them with those of LLM agents. Both groups anticipate mechanisms and use familiar analogies. Qualitative representations are more common in successful human trajectories than in successful LLM trajectories (50.0% versus 14.3%). Humans more often explore unfamiliar situations without a concrete hypothesis, while hypothesis testing is common in both groups. We also trace how learners recover through belief revision, replanning, and execution correction. As LLMs with well-designed harnesses reach saturated performance on public ARC-AGI-3 games, our cognitive analyses motivate next-generation benchmarks that challenge familiar priors, require accumulated evidence and abstraction, and test planning through subgoals, experimentation, and recovery. Our dataset is available at [https://arc3-human-think-aloud.github.io/](https://arc3-human-think-aloud.github.io/).

Cyber threats have become increasingly automated, adaptive, and difficult to manage through conventional rule-based security mechanisms. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-mining techniques offer advanced capabilities for detecting suspicious activities, intrusions, malware, phishing, and anomalous network behavior. However, existing research remains predominantly model-centered and provides limited understanding of how AI-enabled cybersecurity systems are designed, explained, trusted, and used in practice. This study investigates AI-driven cyber-threat detection and chatbot-supported cybersecurity through a sequential mixed-method design. The first stage conducted a bibliometric analysis of publications indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection from 1 January 2016 to 30 April 2026. The 2026 records represent a partial publication year. The analysis examined publication trends, contributing authors, countries, sources, citation patterns, and keyword clusters. The second stage involved semi-structured interviews with 10 developers and 10 users to explore the functionalities, implementation requirements, perceived benefits, and concerns associated with chatbot-supported cybersecurity. The bibliometric findings identified three major research areas: cybersecurity and threat-detection applications, artificial intelligence and machine-learning detection methods, and data-mining-based network-intrusion detection. The qualitative findings indicate that cybersecurity chatbots can provide rapid warnings, explain cyber risks, support phishing identification, offer first-level incident guidance, improve cybersecurity awareness, and escalate serious cases to human specialists. However, participants also identified concerns regarding data quality, privacy, explainability, trust, false positives, false negatives, adversarial manipulation, and overreliance on automated advice. The study proposes a human-centered framework integrating data foundations, detection intelligence, chatbot interaction, developer responsibility, user acceptance, governance, human oversight, and continuous learning. The findings position cybersecurity chatbots as supportive communication and decision-assistance tools rather than replacements for validated detection technologies or cybersecurity professionals.

Extended reality (XR) technologies are increasingly adopted by human factors researchers and practitioners across domains ranging from manufacturing to workplace safety and ergonomics. This interactive XR Showcase session provides attendees with direct, hands-on engagement with XR devices and applications presented by researchers. This year’s demonstrations reflect growing interest in XR applications for skilled manual work and assembly, workplace safety and ergonomics, visualization, and mobility interaction. While training remains an established theme, an emerging trend is the integration of artificial intelligence within XR. Collectively, these demonstrations illustrate a broader shift in the field toward XR platforms that serve not only as visualization tools, but as integrated systems for performance measurement and human-AI collaboration. The XR Showcase advances the goals of HFES by strengthening community interaction and facilitating knowledge exchange among researchers, practitioners, and students interested in the expanding role of XR in human factors research and practice.

As AI systems become increasingly embedded in industrial decision-making, ensuring they support rather than overwhelm human operators has emerged as a critical design challenge. Human factors construct such as cognitive workload, trust calibration, and situation awareness are central to this challenge, yet their empirical evaluation remains inconsistent. This scoping review examined 30 peer-reviewed studies to assess how consistently these constructs, alongside explainability and usability, were evaluated across Industry 4.0, and 5.0 contexts. A co-occurrence analysis revealed a structural misalignment: explainability and trust dominated the evaluation landscape, while cognitive workload and usability remained largely unmeasured. Workload and usability showed zero co-occurrence, and 11 papers (36.7%) reported trust without cognitive or performance validation. No study assessed all five constructs simultaneously. Integrated human-in-the-loop evaluation frameworks incorporating validated measures such as NASA-TLX and SUS are needed to ensure AI-enabled industrial systems are interpretable, cognitively safe, and aligned with Industry 5.0 principles.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, presenting significant challenges in treatment due to tumor heterogeneity, drug resistance, and limitations of conventional preclinical models. Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) offer a transformative platform for addressing these issues. Derived from adult somatic cells, hiPSCs possess pluripotency and self-renewal capabilities, enabling the generation of patient-specific and genetically engineered liver models, including two-dimensional hepatocyte-like cells and more physiologically relevant three-dimensional liver organoids. These hiPSC-derived models are revolutionizing drug development by facilitating high-throughput drug screening, improving the prediction of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), enabling personalized medicine approaches, and elucidating complex disease mechanisms. Despite challenges such as cost, cell maturation state, and scalability, ongoing advancements in culture techniques, microfluidics, and integration with artificial intelligence promise to further enhance the utility of hiPSC technology, holding immense potential for accelerating the discovery of novel therapies and improving patient outcomes in liver cancer.

documents.abstract: Intelligent automation is now used to retrieve information, predict, recommend, generate content, route workflows and take physical or administrative action. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) design is often suggested as a possible fail-safe but it does not necessarily mean that a person is always in control. Oversight can be undermined by lack of time, authority, competence, independent evidence, or feedback or by a lack of real accountability despite the title of oversight. In this paper we explore HITL intelligent automation from three intertwined perspectives: calibrated trust, operational oversight, and workforce implications. It combines existing human-automation research, guidance for human–AI interaction, risk-management standards, regulation, and evidence of labor. A threat model encompasses technical misfortune, adversarial manipulation, cognitive and organizational failure, and harmful deployment of workforce. The mathematical formulation determines the automation modes based on expected error consequence, uncertainty, review cost, workload and skill preservation. The suggested architecture is that of separating the execution of the model from the risk routing, human decision making, dual authorization, audit, appeal, and learning feedback. A seeded synthetic experiment with 10,000 binary decisions is conducted for the comparisons between automation-only, passive universal review, risk-adaptive HITL, and dual control. With the declared generator, adaptive review achieves a 83.6% to 85.0% accuracy rate, while reviewing 37.1% of cases, and dual control achieves a 87.0% accuracy rate with a 5.2% rate of high impact error. These are indicative values and not measurements taken in the workplace. The review finds that effective HITL systems must have meaningful intervention capability, calibrated reliance, representative evaluation, protected worker voice, continuous competence and evidence of oversight functioning under realistic workload and failure.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, has transformed User Experience (UX) and User Interface (UI) design.Traditionally a human-centered discipline built on creativity, empathy, and iterative evaluation, UX design now increasingly involves AI tools that generate interface concepts, recommend components, analyse user behaviour, and support prototyping.Yet limited research examines how UX professionals actually collaborate with AI and what determines successful AI-assisted design practice.This research develops and validates a Human-AI Assisted UI Design Framework (HAUIDF), integrating Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HCAI), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Human-AI Teaming Theory, and Distributed Cognition Theory.The framework links AI transparency, explainability, and design capability; perceived usefulness, ease of use, and human control; AI trust and collaborative creativity; to UX productivity, design quality, designer satisfaction, and continued AI adoption intention.A mixed-method design is proposed: a quantitative survey of 300-400 UX professionals analysed with PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4), complemented by 15-25 semi-structured interviews analysed thematically.The expected contribution is an empirically grounded account of AI as a collaborative design partner rather than an automation tool, offering theoretical contributions to HCI and AI-adoption research and practical guidance for designers, organizations, and AI tool developers pursuing human-centered AI workflows.

While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/

The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity. The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

AIM: To evaluate whether patterns of change derived from routine ward measurements provide additional predictive value beyond the most recent clinical measurements for haemorrhage prediction in general ward patients. DESIGN: A retrospective cohort study. METHODS: Among 16,197 adult patients admitted to general wards in three university-affiliated hospitals in South Korea, 1152 (7.1%) experienced haemorrhage, whereas 15,045 (92.9%) did not. Three machine-learning algorithms evaluated three feature sets based on the most recent clinical measurements, patterns of change or both. Models were trained and internally validated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. Predictive performance was compared across feature sets using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, specificity and F1-score. Shapley Additive Explanations were used to interpret the best-performing model. RESULTS: Models using both recent measurements and patterns of change showed small but statistically supported improvements in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve compared with models using recent measurements alone. Shapley Additive Explanations identified neutrophil count, platelet count, white blood cell count, urine output and vital signs as key predictors. CONCLUSION: Patterns of change derived from routine ward measurements provided complementary predictive information for haemorrhage prediction in general ward patients beyond the most recent clinical measurements. Routinely collected ward data may therefore contain additional predictive information not captured by the most recent values alone. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Machine-learning models combining recent clinical measurements with patterns of change may support risk stratification in general ward patients; prospective evaluation is needed to determine their clinical utility. IMPACT: The study examined whether patterns of change improve haemorrhage prediction. These findings suggest that routinely collected ward data may provide additional predictive information beyond the most recent clinical measurements. The potential value of this information for nursing surveillance and timely intervention warrants prospective evaluation. REPORTING METHOD: Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis-artificial intelligence (TRIPOD + AI).

Large language model (LLM)-based personal agents are increasingly deployed to handle everyday tasks on users' behalf. These agents have access to private user information, while their tasks involve communicating with third parties; this raises a critical privacy concern that agents may inappropriately reveal sensitive user information to these recipients. Existing benchmarks primarily assess direct privacy leakage, where an agent explicitly states a pre-specified secret or attribute. However, they do not capture \textit{inferential leakage}, where the model leaves indirect cues in the reply that implicitly leaks sensitive attributes. We introduce \textsc{InferPriv}, a benchmark that measures whether an honest-but-curious recipient can infer a user's sensitive attributes from an LLM's reply on routine task. Evaluating five frontier models, we find that inferential leakage substantially exceeds direct leakage across models and prompts. Under a privacy-aware system prompt, GPT-6.1-Sol, Sonnet-5.5, and Gemini-3.8-Flash achieve near-zero direct leakage, yet the inferential leakage rate remains between 16.2--25.2\%. These findings suggest that evaluating explicit leakage alone can substantially understate the privacy risks.

This study investigated the relationship between technological, process, and product innovation and employee productivity among employees of selected private higher education institutions (HEIs) in Laoag City, Philippines. It also examined whether age, sex, educational attainment, job tenure, and nature of work moderated the innovation–productivity relationship and developed a strategic action plan for institutional utilization of the findings. The participants were 271 full-time academic and non-academic employees from selected private HEIs. The findings showed that the institutions reported high levels of technological, process, and product innovation and high employee productivity. Process innovation had the strongest positive and statistically significant relationship with employee productivity, while technological innovation had a statistically significant but weaker positive relationship. Product innovation did not have a statistically significant relationship with employee productivity. None of the demographic characteristics significantly moderated the innovation–productivity relationship. The study recommends institutionalizing feasible policies for process innovation, strengthening technology utilization and responsible artificial intelligence integration, refining academic programs through Business Analytics and Artificial Intelligence in Research Methods, and establishing participatory and governance mechanisms that can sustain innovation within existing institutional resources.

ABSTRACT The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into financial services presents a transformative opportunity to advance sustainability goals, yet a systematic understanding of its current state and impact is essential. This review aims to synthesize existing literature on AI applications within the financial sector, emphasizing their role in promoting sustainability and environmental, social, and governance principles. The study screened 3507 articles published in ABS‐ranked journals between 2020 and 2025 on AI and sustainability, narrowing the sample to a core corpus of 181 articles for mixed‐method analysis combining bibliometric techniques with Python‐based data analytics. Synthesized findings reveal significant research prevalence across AI sub‐domains such as machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing within sustainable finance contexts. Although literature supports the potential of AI to act both as an enabler of financial inclusion and as a tool for environmental impact assessment, variations in study contexts suggest a need for further standardized research to fully quantify its long‐term efficacy.

People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

Eye diseases are a leading cause of global vision impairment, yet detection is often hindered by limited resources and geographic barriers. While Deep Learning (DL) offers automated diagnostic solutions, its black-box nature challenges clinical trust. This research investigates whether interpretability can be integrated into DL models for eye disease classification without compromising performance. Using an EfficientNet-B0 architecture, two models were trained on fundus images: one trained only on real images and another incorporating synthetic images generated by a Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN) to simulate insufficient data. Both training approaches were evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation and analysed with eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques: Grad-CAM for visual heatmaps and SHAP for feature-contribution insights. A General Practitioner (GP) also assessed the clinical relevance of selected Grad-CAM outputs. Cross-validation produced mean accuracies of 91.59% ± 0.81% for the real-only model and 90.51% ± 0.83% for the mixed model, with no statistically significant difference in accuracy (paired t-test, p = 0.366). Synthetic image quality was further evaluated using fidelity and diversity metrics, while additional analyses examined classification errors, calibration, and robustness to explanations. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating interpretability with DL models for retinal disease classification, including scenarios involving synthetic data augmentation, supporting further development of transparent and accurate automated medical diagnostic tools.

Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of people of reproductive age, however its influence on career development remains underexplored. This study applies Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT) to examine how endometriosis can shape women’s career development. Using an interpretivist, qualitative design, six semi structured interviews with UK-based women aged 30-39 were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Findings highlight constrained career mobility, revised ambitions, overcompensation, burnout, and concerns about professional reputation, shaped by gendered workplace norms. Supportive management, flexible working, and Occupational Health (OH) provision mitigated these impacts. The study extends SCCT research and offers recommendations for inclusive careers support and workplace practice.

Ranking Atlas Working Paper RA-WP-2026-02. Not peer reviewed. Background. Practitioners widely describe AI engines as a branding channel. In this account, users meet brands in AI answers and then search for them by name on Google. If this holds at scale, US branded search should rise relative to non-branded search as AI adoption grows, and brands that AI engines mention more should gain more. Methods. We froze an analysis plan with three hypotheses (H1a-c) before collecting outcome data, and later added four amendments; two of them added tests of AI recommendation (H2) and recommendation position (H3) after earlier results had been seen. The sample was 347 US brands in 14 categories plus 140 non-branded control terms. AI exposure, top-3 rate and position tier came from 420 ChatGPT and Gemini responses to category prompts (Gemini answers were not US-localised). Outcomes were US branded search in Google Trends (2015-2026) and Google Ads (2022-2026), with pre-AI placebo tests, split-half checks, Holm correction and equivalence tests. Growth is reported in percentage points (pp) of annual growth (log points x 100). Results. No H1 test was supported. The exposure gradient was +2.13 pp per year per SD in Trends (95% CI -0.82 to 5.08) and +2.28 in Ads (95% CI -1.15 to 5.72), and equivalence to zero was not established, so an effect of 2 pp cannot be ruled out. Branded search did not gain share against non-branded search in either source. Brands named among the first three in at least 20% of AI answers grew faster: +7.13 pp per year against matched brands in Ads (95% CI 2.10 to 12.36), with no significant gap in 2015-2022 Trends growth, but the gap was not stable over time. Ads growth was ordered by position tier (+5.42 pp per tier step), but before ChatGPT the ordering tended to run the other way. Under the pre-specified rules both results are inconclusive, and whether first position beats positions 2-3 could not be resolved (11 brands in first position). Conclusions. We found no confirmatory evidence that AI adoption has raised US branded search overall. Brands that AI answers name early show faster recent branded growth, but the top-3 gap was unstable over time and the position ordering tended to reverse a pre-2022 pattern. These patterns are compatible with a modest aggregate echo of individual-level effects reported by industry studies, and also with AI engines favouring already-popular brands. The study does not establish causation.

ISCR-SocioValidate is a Python package with documentation that makes the sociological validation of the Integrated State Cyber Resilience (ISCR) model reproducible. The ISCR model is a seven-layer governance architecture for state cyber resilience under hybrid threats. Its layers are strategic, institutional, operational-coordination, technological, human, legal, and international. The sociological validation asks whether professionals from cybersecurity-relevant sectors accept the model's proposals and which social and organizational preconditions they associate with its implementation. Version 0.1.0 works from a single file of published aggregate survey results (187 of 245 invited professionals) and recomputes every derived statistic and figure of the associated article: 95% Wilson score intervals for top-two-box agreement; an audit of the integer counts consistent with rounded percentages; reliability diagnostics (Cronbach's alpha, Spearman–Brown split-half reliability, implied mean inter-item correlation); a joint display that integrates closed-ended and open-ended evidence across the seven layers, using triangulation categories (agreement, partial agreement, silence, dissonance). Functions for intercoder agreement (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha) and item-level diagnostics prepare a respondent-level mode, which is under development. The record contains the source code, 13 unit tests, the aggregate input file with references to its source tables, a codebook template, generated tables (CSV), and Figures 1–2 (TIFF 800 dpi and PDF). It also includes documentation on the architecture, data schema, an analysis plan aligned with the APA Journal Article Reporting Standards, ethics and data governance, reproducibility, and a roadmap. No respondent-level or personal data are included, and no generative AI is used to code or interpret participants' answers. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later, numpy, pandas, matplotlib. Licence: MIT for code; CC BY 4.0 for documentation and figures.

Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has become a priority in K-12 education, yet frameworks for teaching and assessing it remain fragmented across grade levels, national contexts, and disciplinary traditions. This scoping review maps and synthesizes framework-level contributions to K-12 AI literacy published between January 2024 and December 2025. Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, we searched four databases and grey literature sources, screened 204 unique records, and applied a purpose-built checklist covering five criteria: grade bands, competencies, critical constructs, assessment, and exemplars. Fifty studies met the inclusion threshold. The corpus spans 15 countries, with the United States (32%), Hong Kong (26%), and mainland China (12%) accounting for 70% of included studies. Frameworks defined AI literacy through cognitive, affective, behavioral, ethical, and social dimensions, but dimensional models used inconsistent labels and constructs, with limited crosswalk among them. The ABCE framework offered the closest approximation to a shared measurement tradition, with adaptation across three educational systems. Assessment and curriculum also developed largely in parallel: scale-development papers reported psychometric evidence without instructional sensitivity data, while curriculum papers assessed learning through lesson-linked tools that limited cross-study comparison. Generative AI competencies, including output evaluation, hallucination detection, and prompt design, remained peripheral in most frameworks despite their relevance to students’ everyday encounters with AI. Geographic concentration and limited attention to socioeconomic status, disability, and linguistic diversity further constrained transferability. The field needs stronger convergence through shared vocabulary, curriculum-aligned assessment, longitudinal evidence, and cross-context validation.

Technology-facilitated domestic violence challenges legal systems because everyday digital tools can extend surveillance, intimidation, and coercive control beyond physical encounters. This study examines Indonesia's legal readiness for early detection of technology-facilitated domestic violence, identifies interpretive gaps faced by law enforcement officers, and formulates an operational framework for accountable risk screening. Using a normative-empirical socio-legal approach, the study combines doctrinal analysis of relevant Indonesian laws with thematic analysis of verified interviews involving a Protection of Women and Children police officer, a legal counsel, and a survivor in Gorontalo. The findings show that the principal problem is not an absolute legal vacuum but fragmented legal readiness: relevant norms exist across several legal regimes, while frontline interpretation, digital evidence preservation, institutional capacity, and rapid victim protection remain weakly integrated. The study also identifies procedural fatigue as a factor that may affect survivors' willingness to continue legal processes. Artificial intelligence is positioned as an emerging risk and potential decision-support instrument, not an autonomous legal decision-maker. The study proposes a Five-Dimensional Legal Readiness Framework (KKH-5): normative recognition, interpretive integration, evidentiary readiness, institutional capacity, and protective responsiveness. The framework supports pattern-based interpretation, human oversight, due process, and survivor-centred early intervention.

Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how data-driven research is produced. As AI tools make information and technical execution more accessible, mentorship must concentrate on judgment, ethics, and the design of end-to-end AI-augmented workflows. Disciplinary experts need mentoring to adopt AI while preserving their expertise and human agency, and AI-native research trainees need mentoring to become polymathic workflow developers. This chapter proposes Everyone's Backyard, an interdisciplinary model in which disciplinary experts, trainees, and community partners mentor one another in both directions and across disciplines through shared research practice in a convergence studio. The model centers on four capacities: statistical thinking, data ethics, collaboration, and AI for social good and society. We illustrate the model with the Spring 2026 aiX Faculty Fellows Program at Columbia University, which brought together 20 faculty fellows and 15 student interns from 14 schools and departments. Evaluation data show growth in faculty confidence, intern competence, and cross-disciplinary connection.

The widespread integration of artificial intelligence (AI)–driven communication agents, particularly large language models, has brought about a paradigm shift in communication research. Traditional human-centered paradigms are becoming inadequate for analyzing the behaviors and impacts of these non-human agents, which exhibit autonomous and intelligent communicative capabilities. This article advocates for the development of a Machine Behavior Paradigm in communication studies. This proposed paradigm explicitly expands the disciplinary scope by integrating machine behavior into three core dimensions. About research objects, it emphasizes the shifts from a human-only focus to a dual focus on humans and intelligent machines as communicative subjects. For research approaches, it should expand beyond human–human relationships to encompass machine–machine and hybrid human–machine interactions. In methodologies, we advocate to integrate computational indicators, such as text-generation temperature and activity frequency, alongside traditional empirical tools to address the opacity of AI “black boxes.” Furthermore, the article examines the limitations of current communication theories, such as agenda-setting and the spiral of silence, when applied to AI-driven environments. Also, we argue that it is difficult to study opaque AI systems with traditional methodologies. This shift necessitates interdisciplinary collaboration and the establishment of robust ethical guidelines to ensure the responsible study of autonomous agents. By outlining a systematic framework for individual, collective, and hybrid machine behavior, this article provides a roadmap for future inquiry.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) has recently emerged as a powerful tool with significant potential torevolutionize education, bringing about fundamental changes in pedagogy and research. Its applicationsspan various domains within academia, including administration, instructional method enhancement, andgrade prediction. This study illustrates how ML can enhance the effectiveness of research, instruction,and study strategies by adapting to student needs and leveraging new communication tools within virtuallearning environments. The literature review encompasses various empirical studies outlining theintegration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and ML within the educational sector. This research paper mapsout how educators are leveraging these capabilities while documenting the associated risks and learningoutcomes across various educational tiers. You can also refer to the original context in the file named'Suhani Research Paper OG.pdf' for a comprehensive view. We advocate that current educationalpractices in engineering and computing with GenAI can indicate to us a roadmap of its potentialities,uses, and risks from the standpoint of both teachers and students. Our purpose with the outcomes andconclusions of this scoping review is to support educators, faculty members, and other stakeholders inengineering and computing education to co-create educational methodologies that articulate GenAI withcurricula, AI literacy, and prompt engineering encompassing students’ learning domains such ascognitive, affective, or behavioral. This sample paper is mapped against the IJREK standard studenttemplate format and expands on the empirical findings
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Hassaniya, the Arabic dialect of Mauritania, has almost no machine translation (MT) resources and no standard orthography, and it is among the weakest varieties for current large language models on recent dialectal Arabic benchmarks. A usable Hassaniya translator would let its speakers reach digital, financial, and public services in their own language. We report how we built one in two steps. We first fine-tuned NLLB-200 (1.3B) for English↔Hassaniya on about 25k sentence pairs; it reaches 59.4 chrF++ into English but only 41.5 into Hassaniya. English proves a poor pivot, since it does not mark the gender or politeness that Hassaniya requires when addressing someone. We therefore switch to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and fully fine-tune the Apache-2.0 model MADLAD-400 3B for Hassaniya↔MSA, with a new language tag, on four small parallel corpora (26.7k pairs after cleaning and leakage removal). To measure what each corpus contributes, we train four cumulative models and score them on a test set with an equal share from every corpus, using chrF++, spBLEU, and a copy rate that counts untranslated outputs. Zero-shot, MADLAD-400 copies 90.2% of its MSA inputs instead of producing Hassaniya. The final model reaches 48.0 chrF++ / 34.8 spBLEU for MSA→Hassaniya and 59.3 / 48.0 for Hassaniya→MSA, gains of +21.4 / +23.9 and +31.5 / +33.7 over the base model, and its copy rate falls to 6.9% (human references: 3.5%). Every corpus improves the overall score significantly, but gains are largely confined to each corpus’s own domain. A small conversational service corpus gives the largest gain after the first, and two corpora interfere in the direction that generates Hassaniya. The translator now powers a public Hassaniya chatbot that pivots through MSA to a general-purpose large language model.

Materials research relies on scattered and growing data, knowledge, and simulation tools, and a single study often spans multi-day workflows across literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with new capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost-score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, it outperforms Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. Code is available at https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS.

Large pillar-to-pillar (P2P) displays are replacing traditional instrument clusters, but their visual richness may impair visual search and increase driver distraction. We examined how visual properties of large automotive displays relate to perceived clutter and search performance using subjective, objective, and behavioral measures. Fifty-five participants viewed 18 AI-generated dashboard videos, completed a detection task, and rated clutter, density, overlap, colorfulness, and brightness; corresponding objective metrics were computed from video frames. Subjective density and overlap best predicted clutter, while overlap, edge density, and colorfulness predicted search time. Factor analysis revealed two dimensions, spatial complexity and surface appearance, showing that spatial properties primarily drive clutter perception and that objective metrics can support early-stage interface screening.
